Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Level 2, 121 Macquarie Street,
Sydney, New South Wales
Tuesday, 23 July 2024 at 10.00am
(Day 037)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ian Fraser (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Daniel Fuller (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Richard Cheney SC with Mr Hilbert Chiu for NSW Health

THE COMMISSIONER: Good morning.
MR FRASER: Good morning Commissioner, the next witness is
Dr Nicholas Spooner, the current president of ASMOF, the
Australian Salaried Medical Officers Federation. He's on
screen.
THE COMMISSIONER: Okay. Dr Spooner, hello.
DR SPOONER: Good morning. Thank you for having me.
THE COMMISSIONER: No problem. The screen has frozen but
we can hear you. Can you hear me?
DR SPOONER: I can hear you.
<NICHOLAS ALEXANDER SPOONER, sworn: [10.01am]
<EXAMINATION BY MR FRASER:
MR FRASER: Q. Dr Spooner, can you hear and see me?
A. I can hear and see you.
Q. Thank you. If at any time you can't make out what
we're saying, please let us know. Thank you very much.
Could you please give your full name?
A. It is Nicholas Alexander Spooner.
Q. Is it right you are currently the director of
emergency medicine at Wyong Hospital; is that right?
A. That's correct.
Q. And currently the president of the Australian Salaried
Medical Officers Federation; is that right?
A. Yes, that's correct.
Q. Dealing with each of those and then I will take you to
some other things, firstly, when were you elected as
president of ASMOF?
A. End of May, and then appointed by the registrar of the
IRC in the beginning of June of this year.
Q. So you are in your second month in office,
effectively?
A. Correct, very fresh.
Q. And can I also, in relation to your substantive

medical position, when were you appointed director of
emergency medicine at Wyong?
A. That would be the beginning of last year, so about one
year ago, and prior to that was the deputy director here
for about three years.
Q. And your underlying appointment, is that right, is
that you are a staff specialist in emergency medicine?
A. That's correct.
Q. And, of course, Wyong Hospital is within the Central
Coast Local Health District; is that correct?
A. Yes, that's correct.
Q. Dr Spooner, you provided the Inquiry with a statement
[SCI.0011.0249.0001] dated 17 July; is that right?
A. Correct.
Q. Have you got access to a copy of it, should you
require it?
A. Yes, I do.
Q. And before giving evidence this morning have you read
through it?
A. Yes, I have.
Q. Is there anything within it that you wish to change,
alter?
A. Not at the moment, thank you.
Q. So it's true and correct to the best of your
knowledge; is that right?
A. Correct.
MR FRASER: Commissioner, that will form part of the bulk
tender in due course.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MR FRASER: Q. And just to round out a few bits of
background, you tell us in your statement that prior to
becoming a staff specialist, you completed most of your
training in the Central Coast Local Health District; is
that right?
A. That's correct.
Q. So overall, you've worked there in one capacity or

another, how long do you think?
A. About 14 years - about 13 years, from 2011. I think
I said I'm the exclusive product of NSW Health from
a medicine perspective.
Q. And in terms of your background prior to medicine, did
you have another discipline or field of work before
becoming a doctor?
A. Yes, I was an aerospace engineer in Canada and I did
a masters in biomedical engineering in Canada as well and
then took a fancy for medicine and have come to Australia
to pursue that career.
Q. So you did your degree here as well?
A. My medical degree, correct.
Q. You tell us in your statement as well at paragraph 7
that other than your personal experiences at Wyong and
within the Central Coast Local Health District, to
extrapolate from that generally, you are speaking on behalf
of ASMOF as well as yourself; is that right?
A. Yes, that's correct.
Q. The first thing I would like to take you to are what
you have termed "current workforce issues", and I will take
to you some illustrations within your statement at your
local health district. You have said in paragraph 8 that
it's your view that the current workforce model in
New South Wales is outdated and is regularly unable to
provide a sufficient workforce?
A. Yes, that's correct. So out of step with the current
demand and even in its sort of suboptimal workforce
modelling, we're unable to fill all the positions on the
roster presently.
Q. We'll come back to the "why" in a moment. From your
statement, before we go to the specifics, that's your
personal experience as well as that of ASMOF; is that
right?
A. Yes, that's correct, both.
Q. And at the moment we're talking predominantly about
the medical workforce?
A. I would - yes, correct. Anecdotally my experience is
similar across allied health and nursing, but there will be
people who can attest to that with more credence than I.

Q. I will ask you now about the medical workforce, and
we'll just get some terms locked down. You're a staff
specialist which, for those - aren't you, Dr Spooner?
A. Yes, I am.
Q. That's right. And for those watching along who may
not be aware, a staff specialist is an employed consultant;
is that correct?
A. Yes, that's right.
Q. And you've also referred in your statement to visiting
medical officers, otherwise known as VMOs; is that right?
A. Yes, correct. Yes, that's right.
Q. And your understanding is they are contracted
consultants; is that right?
A. That's right.
Q. With contracts with NSW Health?
A. That's correct.
Q. And there are two types, you understand, of VMOs; is
that right?
A. Yes, conventionally those who are on a contract with
the hospital for a longer period of time and those who come
in a locum capacity for much shorter stints, and the locum
capacity often attracts locum agency fees and travel and
accommodation fees as well.
Q. And within VMO, those with contracts, you have -
although you are not one, you understand that some are
contracted to provide on a sessional basis and some are on
a fee for service basis; is that right?
A. Yes, that's correct.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. Can I just ask you, Dr Spooner, in
paragraph 9, you say there are multiple full-time
equivalent positions vacant. In paragraph 10, you talk of
13 vacancies in the medical staff roster in the ED, and in
11, 10 full-time equivalent vacancies at the middle grade,
ie, registrars in the ED. Can I just go back to
paragraph 9. The multiple full-time equivalent FTE
positions, are you referring to the positions you later,
subsequently, refer to in 10 and 11?
A. Not exactly, and I would be happy to clarify.
Q. Yes, please do.

A. So in 9 I referred to full-time equivalent positions
that are vacant, that's in the staff specialist roster, the
very senior roster. Presently, at our hospital, there's
roughly four or five FTEs vacant in my department.
Q. For staff specialists?
A. That's correct, yes.
Q. That's staff specialists in different disciplines?
A. Emergency.
Q. All in emergency?
A. Only in my department, in emergency. And in
paragraph 10, this was in the midst of the COVID-19
pandemic, there were many days when our daily roster sheet
showed the number of doctors who were coming to work in the
emergency department on the day, where there were many,
many, many blank lines, no doctor available to come to
work.
Q. Was that because of the pandemic largely or
a combination of other things?
A. It was multifactorial. The pandemic certainly didn't
help with travel restrictions, and certainly
geographically, the Central Coast and certainly the
northern part of the Central Coast in Wyong is
a challenging area to recruit to when workforce labour
market is strained.
Q. Just before I come back to that, in 11, you're talking
about a different set of vacancies; rather than staff
specialists you're talking about the registrars?
A. That is correct.
Q. Right. Why is the Central Coast, do you think,
a challenging area to recruit to?
A. I guess it's geographically pigeonholed between
Newcastle and Sydney and those larger metropolitan centres
have on offer, for people, urban attractions that sometimes
outweigh the more regional centres, and when the regional
areas are areas that can be developed from a residential
point of view at a lower cost, that means that we have more
lower socioeconomic status, more housing communities being
built, difficult access to primary care where people are
relying on hospital and the emergency department for many
aspects of their care, so it is multifactorial but the
gravitation --

Q. Do you mean, sorry, relying on the ED not just for
acute care that it's meant for but for care that might
ordinarily be provided by a general practitioner in a
private practice, for example?
A. Yes, correct.
Q. I mean, tell me if you've got to guess and I'll still
allow you to guess, but how much of your ED has patients
that are coming in that could easily be seen or
appropriately be seen by a general practitioner as distinct
from actually having a condition or an injury that requires
them to be seen in an ED?
A. Yeah,, it would be a guess, but I can get the numbers
more definitively to you, but somewhere between sort of
10 and 20 per cent, I would say.
Q. Can you make a note to see if you can get that, the
most accurate data you can for us, in relation to that?
A. Certainly.
Q. Before I ask you a question on another different
topic, what in your view is the cause - I mean, there is
perhaps an obvious reason but what's the cause of so many
people presenting to your ED that could be seen by
a general practitioner?
A. They are again, multifactorial. So obviously people
need to seek their health care from somewhere when they are
worried, in their time of need, they are going to go to
a place that they know is open, they are going to go to
a place that, in their experience, has all of the services
in one spot.
If they do attend their general practitioner and they
need blood tests or radiology imaging or some other
consultation, that is done as an outpatient to and from the
GP clinic, and you visit other medical sort of modalities.
In emergency and in hospital we have access to all of those
at our fingertips which makes us very attractive for those
who have engaged with the health system in another way and
felt that it was clunky and inefficient. Coming to the ED
where we have everything is particularly efficient, but the
waiting times become challenging when we're trying to
process so many patients. But certainly the attraction is
all the modalities in one spot with an emergency physician
and other consultants available for advice.

Q. Bearing in mind your position, do you still get to
know the GPs in your general geographic area?
A. Not as much as we would like and not as much as in
recent past, which is unfortunate and frustrating.
Q. Is there a reason for that?
A. I would say work intensification across the board for
everyone means that those human factors are put to the
side.
Q. Do you know whether the GPs in your general geographic
area - do they have their books full? Do you know if there
are enough GPs to meet the demand for general practitioner
type services in your area?
A. My anecdotal experience is the answer is no, patients
are often - when we say "You'll need to follow up with your
GP for this", they retort that they may find that
challenging to get into at short notice.
Q. And could I ask you, in paragraph 9 you say, "Despite
determined attempts to attract and retain staff to fill"
the position you are discussing - what are those determined
attempts? Can you give me some idea?
A. So the options that we have available to us are to put
out applications to go to the labour market and see what's
out there for all facets of fractions, so you could work as
a 1 FTE fraction, you could work in a 0.5, you could work
whatever suits you. We can do that as a VMO, we can do
that as a staff specialist. We are particularly flexible,
certainly in this labour market, to take whatever we are
able to get that satisfies the requirements and even
despite that we are unable to fill all of our positions.
Q. I know I did ask you before but do you get feedback
specifically in relation to those attempts about why you
can't fill those positions or is it the same answer you
gave previously to a similar question?
A. Yeah, rarely do we get feedback. Mostly it's just
a limited pool of applicants.
Q. And can I ask you, are these positions advertised on
the LHD's website or --
A. They are advertised broadly, consistent with the
district's approach for advertising, and that's oftentimes
in journals, oftentimes electronically through the college
that the position is associated with so we - and those come
at expense as well, so we attempt to engage in all the

common-day reasonably productive modalities to get us the
best set of recruits or set of people who are interested,
candidates.
We also use sort of internal comms between different
departments and different LHDs to put the feelers out for
people personally to ask their friends or other groups they
may be on to message, to get the ads out.
Q. And what's the consequence of having the level of
vacancies you have mentioned (a) in relation to staff
specialists; and then (b) if it's a slightly different
answer, in relation to registrars?
A. So I guess globally, if you are trying to do the work
that is necessary and give the care that is necessary and
you don't have the resources required to do that, you
either have to have intensification of work, which impacts
fatigue and morale and culture, and that's sustainable for
a small period of time, we all know that we can work hard
for a short time, but it's not indefinitely sustainable and
then something's got to give.
The alternative, which is somewhat even more
frustrating, is you're unable to give the care that you
would like to give because you don't have the resources
that you need and then patients suffer and then, obviously,
the second victim syndrome of the staff suffering because
they knew that they couldn't give morally what they knew
was right to patients because of the resourcing challenges.
Q. What do you mean specifically by you can't give the
care you want to give. Does it mean there's more time to
wait for the patient or does it mean something beyond that?
A. It is both. So initially, what happens is time.
People who can wait, do wait, and that's the nature of the
triage system for emergency engagement. People who can
wait, do wait.
Then, subsequently, when the resources are even more
stretched and the acuity is high for several patients, it
means that some patients may get a delay to care that we
would like to see them have more urgently and that's
insidious in its beginning and then becomes - when the
resources are stretched further, that becomes even more
identifiable, delays, whether to medications, delay to
could be antibiotics, it could be analgesia, it could be
consultations of a specialist, it could be transport to

another hospital for definitive care when there are many,
many competing interests. Unfortunately humans can only do
one at a time, and if we don't have enough people to do one
at a time for every person then somebody has to wait and
they may be waiting for something that's emergent.
Q. So there are at least four factors, there might be
more, but three for the medical professionals, one is
becoming fatigued and stretched, I will just use that term.
A. Yes.
Q. And secondly, then there's the general concern as
a medical professional that provides health services of not
being able to give perhaps the quality or timely care you
want to give; and then there's at least two consequences
for the patient. One is having to wait longer than perhaps
is desirable, but also for those patients that have a more
acute need, a delay in providing that acute level care
that, the preference, at least from the medical
practitioner, is that they are given it earlier?
A. That's correct.
Q. Is that a general --
A. That's correct.
MR FRASER: Q. Just to clarify a few things about the
size of that deficiency, you said in answer to some
questions from the Commissioner that you currently have
four or five FTE consultant level positions vacant?
A. In Wyong emergency, yes, and that's one of many, many,
many departments across our Central Coast and the
NSW Health.
Q. Indeed, and I will come to that in a moment, just to
put that in terms of the scale, how many consultants do you
have positions for within the ED?
A. So my established FTE is roughly 19.5. That's rounded
to 20.
Q. So between 20 and 25 per cent of your consultant
positions are currently vacant; is that right?
A. Correct.
Q. And you have spoken in paragraph 11 of 10 FTE
vacancies at what you've termed the middle grade, and let's
just clarify that. When you term registrars, you're
differentiating them obviously from consultants at the top

end; is that right?
A. No, registrars - consultants sit outside the registrar
cohort, the middle grade cohort, so --
Q. Yes, but when you say "middle, what are they in the
middle off? Junior medical officers at the bottom; is that
right?
A. Yes, correct, JMOs - junior medical officers - at the
bottom and consultants at the top, yes, correct.
Q. Yes, that's what I was coming to. And in terms of
registrars, how many FTEs are in your established
structure?
A. Roughly 30 --
Q. So you are missing approximately --
A. -- in the ED at Wyong.
Q. In your ED, so approximately 30, 33 per cent of --
A. Roughly, yes, correct.
Q. And just in terms of how long that sort of scale has
been the case, you tell us in your statement - and I know
you've only been the director for a year, but you have
worked in the ED for at least five years; is that right?
A. Yes, correct, and then for several years before then
as a trainee, correct.
Q. How long has it been that size of a deficiency in your
vacancies?
A. At least since my time as an emergency physician, so
at least five years, and probably then some, and just
slowly the gap growing.
Q. Thank you. You've made the point that this is within
your department within your particular hospital. You've
made some illustrations in paragraph 11 of some of your
colleagues within the local health district - 10, a similar
number as you, 10 FTE vacant registrar positions at Gosford
ED?
A. Correct.
Q. And you also have indicated an understanding of
4.5 FTE short in obstetrics and gynaecology. Is that
across the district or a particular location?
A. That's across the district and that's from my ASMOF
experience.

Q. And just putting your ASMOF hat on, is it your
understanding that these shortfalls are replicated in other
places?
A. That's certainly my understanding.
Q. Can we just come back --
A. And I would just clarify that it's probably more
disparate in the regional and rural areas as compared to
urban, but certainly that's ubiquitous - shortfalls are
ubiquitous across the state.
Q. And one exception, perhaps, to that is that which you
have highlighted at the end of paragraph 11, which is the
shortfall in psychiatrists at the Western Sydney Local
Health District; is that right?
A. Correct. Psychiatry on a whole is about 25 per cent
under-recruited and some of that is disproportionately in
certain areas of the state, who are feeling the brunt,
correct.
Q. Out of interest, do you know what the position is in
your local health district for psychiatry?
A. I do not know, I'm sorry.
Q. That's all right. Now, in your statement you have
spoken of the efforts to fill those gaps. You have spoken
already to the Commissioner about the different modes of
attempt, advertisements, in an attempt to recruit to
positions, and I think in answer to a question from the
Commissioner you've said generally, just not sufficient
applicants of the required standard to fill all the
positions; is that right?
A. Correct.
Q. And in paragraph 12 you give an example of that of
a four-week period in May 2024 where there were, according
to your statement, 45 vacant consultant shifts within the
medical staff roster in your ED?
A. Correct.
Q. And you sought to fill those with either VMOs or locum
staff?
A. Correct.
Q. And you managed to fill just over half.
A. That's right.

Q. Is that representative of your experience sort of
month to month?
A. Yes, it is. And I would just also add that
the workforce modelling that we are trying to fill is out
of step with the current demand as well
Q. I'll just take you to that. You dealt with that in
your statement. When you say "out of step", can you tell
us what you mean by that?
A. So the workforce models that are put in place about
how many staff we should have in order to deliver a service
are based on estimates of population growth and demand
coming to the hospital and through each of the departments
across all of the state. And the strategic plans for
districts are put in place to try to address what they
expect demand to look like over the coming three, four or
five years, and in our experience, the workforce models
that have been funded are not in step with the demand that
we are actually seeing, so they often - there is a more
conservative approach to what the workforce models are
funded to rather than what we are seeing as populations
increase and presentations grow.
Q. Just because it is illustrative, you have dealt in
your statement at paragraph 25 with a model that is for
emergency departments that has been compiled or authored by
your college, the Australasian College For Emergency
Medicine; is that right?
A. Yes, that's correct.
Q. We'll just put that up on the screen, if we may,
[SCI.0011.0242.0001]. Hopefully that will come up. It's
referred to as the G23 guidelines. You are not
a contributor to this document, are you, Dr Spooner?
A. I have not.
Q. But you are familiar with it, presumably?
A. I am.
Q. And in terms of its - in your opinion as a director
of emergency department, do the numbers seem generally
about right, in your opinion? We'll come to --
A. Yes, and the incredible amount of work that the
college has put into that, I feel very comfortable with it.
Q. If we just come to, because we've been talking about

Wyong, if we go to page 7 of that document, on that page it
deals with recommended levels of medical staffing for
emergency departments --
A. Yes.
Q. -- on that page and over. And per shift. It's split
into three shifts - day shift, evening shift and, over the
page, night shift. Is that the way that your shifts are
split?
A. Yes, correct, day, evening and night.
Q. Thank you. It's formulated on the basis of emergency
presentations per annum in the left-hand column, and if we
look at the day shift, for example, approximately how many
presentations are at your ED?
A. I would say just under 80,000. This year we may very
well go over 80, so - but to be conservative, we should be
looking at between 65,000 and 80,000 for my emergency
department.
THE COMMISSIONER: Can I just ask you, I can see this on
the screen, but can you tell me where it is in the bundle?
MR FRASER: Yes, Commissioner, it is behind - it is H --
THE COMMISSIONER: I have H1 and H2, both of which have
multiple volumes.
MR FRASER: H7.7. It's directly behind Dr Spooner's
statement.
THE COMMISSIONER: Here it is, sorry, yes. I've found the
volume. Yes, I have that, thanks.
MR FRASER: And we're on page 7, Commissioner.
Q. So this table, Dr Spooner, provides recommendations at
the different levels. If we can just deal with that,
"Expert" or "FACEM" - those are your consultants; is that
right?
A. Correct.
Q. And the more junior doctors are split into three
levels, advanced, intermediate and basic. From what you
said, we were discussing earlier, is it right you divide
those doctors into two in your --
A. Yes, correct. That's the way that we do our

modelling, but I anticipated you would like to talk about
that and I'm happy to talk about it in the capacity that we
can see it on the screen.
Q. All right.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. The term "modelling" that's being
used, can I just ask, the document we're looking at, the
"Constructing a Sustainable Emergency Department Medical
Workforce", is this document the result of some form of
simulation or predictive modelling or is it more
a guideline as to the medical staffing that might be needed
for an ED depending on how many presentations there are in
a year?
A. I suspect the latter. I was not specifically involved
in it. Predictive modelling analytics, if you're referring
to more analytics might be --
Q. Those sort of analytics would be more likely to be
used where you're actually looking at a specific population
and you've got the data about its age profile,
socioeconomic demographics, you know, levels of chronic
disease - all those sorts of things - where you might then
feed that into a model and say, "This is what we're likely
going to need", because there might be a population of
100,000 in a certain area with all of those certain
demographics that might have far less or far more
presentations to an ED than another population of 100,000
because of different age profile and other things
I mention; correct?
A. Yes, correct.
THE COMMISSIONER: Okay.
MR FRASER: It is a blunter tool, Commissioner.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes, that's not a criticism, because
it's a general thing, it's not looking at a specific
population as far as I can gather, having seen this
document two minutes ago for the first time.
MR FRASER: Q. Dr Spooner, if we just work our way
across, the 65,000 to 80,000 line, this recommends five
consultants on a day shift. How many do you have --
THE COMMISSIONER: Which table am I looking at, 6.1?

MR FRASER: Table 6.1.
THE WITNESS: Yes, so we have roughly 2.5, and I know that
sounds like a strange number - sorry, 3.5. That sounds
like a strange number. We have a shift that crosses over
between day and evening to help to capture the time of day
that has more patients presenting.
MR FRASER: Q. I think in your statement you've referred
to two. Is that two at the beginning but picked up with
some more with the crossover; is that right?
A. That's correct.
Q. And in terms of the more junior doctors, it recommends
11 in total, but made up of those levels. What is the
position at Wyong on a day shift?
A. Roughly nine. And I would just reiterate the
challenge is that's what we are funded for, but we're
unable to fill those positions, so what we actually see on
the floor is not even what we are funded for.
Q. And how many vacancies of that might you have?
A. Sometimes one or two a day and sometimes up to five or
six and sometimes during COVID - and I appreciate that was
a long time ago - sometimes up to 13.
Q. That would leave you with no-one.
A. Across the whole day, I'm sorry.
Q. Across the whole day, I see.
A. Yes.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. Can I just ask you, in
paragraph 24 of your statement where you're talking about
predictive workforce modelling, in the last sentence you
say:
... I believe it is viewed as something of
a novel concept by NSW Health.
I want to ask you what the basis of that belief is, but
before I do, predictive or simulation modelling is not new
science. I know that from having worked for a bookmaker
many years ago and an interest in horse racing. I know
predictive modelling is not new science, not that there's
a ready analogy to health care, but this isn't new science.
What is the basis of your belief that it is a novel concept

to NSW Health?
A. Some years ago I did ask myself if we had a bucket of
money or access to extra nursing staff or access to extra
doctors, I asked myself where would the best place be for
them to go to work, should they go and work in nursing
homes to get patients out of hospital; should they go to
work on wards to get patients in the hospital from the
emergency department; should they work in the emergency
department? And I asked myself - I didn't have the
capacity just in my own brain to figure out where the best
place was for them to work and I thought, as you've
inferred from bookmaking or horse racing or manufacturing
and what-not, there may be a way to try to do where the
best cost-effective place for them to go to work was.
And so I was curious about that, and asked through our
executive channels whether or not we had any - had been
doing any or whether or not that was a thought about
predictive analytics and the answer was no, we hadn't, that
there was none of that being done presently.
Q. I think I know the answer to this but I'll ask it
anyway: would you see a benefit in that sort of predictive
simulation or modelling being done for different LHDs on
the basis that some are going to have similar demographics
for their populations but others might have quite
different, which those sort of modelling tools might be of
an advantage to work out what workforces might be needed,
as an example, in EDs?
A. I guess the pragmatic answer is if there - sorry, the
answer is yes. We should explore the options to ensure
that we're using our resources as efficiently as possible.
I guess the pragmatic answer is if the resources aren't
present, then is that an exercise in futility, and that's
rhetorical. Of course, we should try to gather more
information about how we should use our existing resources.
Q. I mean, I guess past patient number presentations from
the year before to an ED are a reasonable guide as to what
